summary: Describes a project to build a single-access-point service for searching for whitepages information on Swedish Internet users. It covers the technical infrastructure for directory gateways. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2967 describes a Swedish project to build one front door for telephone-directory searches. The gateway holds only a list of which provider knows about which people, and sends each search on to the right provider, so no one's data is copied and no user has to guess which provider to ask.

questions: what is the swedish directory access gateway
subtitle: One front door for looking up Swedish telephone-directory information, without copying anyone's data

tldr.problem: Swedish directory service providers each ran their own protocol and their own database, so a user searching for a person had to try one service after another, each with different search rules and different answers.
tldr.mechanism: The DAG keeps an index of who holds which records rather than the records themselves. A query arrives in any of five client protocols, is translated into one internal protocol, matched against the index, and the answer is either a referral to the provider or, where the client cannot handle referrals, a chained query performed on the user's behalf.
tldr.outcome: Users get the same information and the same availability whichever provider holds it, and providers keep control of their own data and their own value-added services. The memo is an Informational record of a project, not a standard.

facts.label: Client access protocols
facts.value: 5: SMTP, HTTP, LDAPv2, Whois++ and LDAPv3

facts.label: Search types supported
facts.value: 6 combinations of name, role, organization and locality

today: RFC 2967 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the technical design of a Swedish project rather than a standard, and its own requirement was that the system would be operational by the end of 1998.

sections.title: The Project and Its Goal
sections.content:
The overarching goal of the TISDAG project is to develop the technical infrastructure for a single-access-point service for searching whitepages information on Swedish Internet users. The service must be uniform for all information: the same level of access to the information, on a 7x24 basis, and the same information made available, whichever provider maintains it, whichever directory service protocol it uses, and whichever access protocol the end user's software speaks.

The strength of the proposal, in the words of the memo, is that instead of requiring centralized mirroring of complete information records from Swedish directory service providers, the system uses a well-defined index object summary of that data, updated at each provider's convenience. When a user queries, the referral information is used, either by the user's own software or by a module inside the gateway as appropriate, to complete the final query directly at the provider's system. That way the user gets the most up-to-date complete information, and the provider's main interest, its own service, is promoted. The architecture is also modular, so support for future protocols can be added in the operational system.

The memo has five parts. Requirements capture what the different users of the service need, which in turn defines the constraints on the system. The functional specification works from those requirements to a conceptual architecture. The architecture section specifies a software architecture that meets the functionality and the requirements. The software specifications then give the details for each component, and the service specifications cover the operational characteristics on which the success of the service rests.

The vocabulary is short. The DAG system is the collection of infrastructural software and services for providing unified access to Swedish whitepages information. The DAG-CAP is the Client Access Point, the point of communication between client access software and the system. The DAG-SAP is the Service Access Point, the point of communication between the DAG and the whitepages directory service provider's software. DAG/IP is the internal protocol used between the components of the DAG. A WDSP is a Whitepages Directory Service Provider, an ISP, company or other interested entity. Whitepages information is the collected coordinates for individual people, typically a name and an e-mail address.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is a gateway in the middle. It does not hold the directory data; it holds an index saying which provider knows about which person. A search arrives in whatever protocol the user's software speaks, and the gateway works out which providers to ask.

sections.title: What the Two Kinds of User Need
sections.content:
There are two primary classes of user. End-users are people performing whitepages searches through various forms of client software. WDSPs are the providers themselves, who are already in the business of supplying whitepages information and have requirements that must be respected for the service to be useful to everyone.

The end-user is offered a specific set of search types: name; name plus organization; role plus organization; name plus locality; name plus organization plus locality; and role plus organization plus locality. Where available, the results for each hit include the full name, e-mail address, role, organization, locality, full address and telephone numbers. Access has to be through reasonable and current protocols, so that directory-aware software can use the service seamlessly, and responses are expected to be timely: a standard search should take no longer than the average access to a web server.

The provider's requirements are about fairness and effort. The system must give reasonable assurances of data integrity, so that what the user sees corresponds directly to what the provider supplied, and it must be non-preferential in providing whitepages information: the service is to the end-user, and the source of the information should not influence the search and the way results are presented. It must reflect information updates within a reasonable time of receiving them from providers, while the update and participation overhead for a provider must stay within reasonable bounds of what it should already be doing to support regular access to its information. And because providers supply their information with an eye to value-added service, end-users should be redirected wherever possible to the provider responsible for the individual directory entry for final and further information.

The system itself carries its own design constraints. It must be implementable and operational by the end of 1998, which implies building on technologies that already existed. It will have participation requirements such as 7x24 availability from providers. In terms of scale it should handle 8 million records at the outset, with a view to larger systems later, and it must be capable of extension to other related applications, such as serving security certificate information.
sections.plainLanguage: Users want one search box that works the same whatever is behind it. Providers want their data to arrive unchanged, their own services to be what the user ends up at, and their workload to stay small. The system has to be built from parts that already existed and handle millions of records.

sections.title: What the Client Sees
sections.content:
The gateway answers queries arriving over e-mail (SMTP), the web (HTTP), LDAPv2, Whois++ and LDAPv3. For protocols that can handle referrals, the response is data and or referrals in that protocol; those are Whois++ and LDAPv3. Because not every client can handle every access protocol, only referrals to LDAPv3 servers are returned.

User input is defined in terms of searchable attributes, matching semantics and character sets. The system supports fragment-matching queries on a limited set of attributes: name, organizational role, organization and locality, in six permitted combinations, which are the same six search types listed as the end-user requirements. The role-based queries are separated from the rest because they are searches for virtual persons, roles within an organization such as a president or a customer service desk, for which someone might want contact information. The matching semantics expected to be available in all client access software are full word exact match, word substring match, so that cat matches scatter, and both case-sensitive and case-insensitive matching. The memo argues from the LDAP and X.500 experience that the referral index should be case-insensitive, with case sensitivity supported by the service access points where the native access protocol supports it.

Character sets are handled with Unicode version 2.0, specifically the UTF-8 encoding, wherever possible, with accommodation made where necessary for the deployed base of existing software. All internal communications over DAG/IP are carried out in UTF-8. The client access points must support UTF-8 where the access protocol lets the client select a character set, and may support others. The service access points must support UTF-8 and use it whenever the remote provider supports it, and the index objects the providers supply must contain data encoded in UTF-8.

The output schema is deliberately minimal: a basic information schema carrying what the service needs and no more, because the more detailed the presentation, the harder it is to map the schema across protocols with different paradigms. Each client access point defines how it expresses that schema in its own protocol. Error handling is minimal too: each access point must support an unrecognized query and too many hits, and may refuse a query by redirecting the user to another access point of the same protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Five ways in: e-mail, the web, two versions of LDAP and Whois++. Only six searches are supported, and the matching rules are simple: exact word, part of a word, and either case-sensitive or not. Text is UTF-8 throughout, and the record returned is deliberately small so it can be translated into any of the protocols.

sections.title: The Architecture and Its Two Jobs
sections.content:
Communications between the components of the gateway run over TCP/IP connections using DAG/IP. That internal protocol defines the range of query the client access points can express to the referral index, the format of the index's answers, the range of query the access points can express to the service access points when chasing a referral, and the format of those answers. No module outside the system should know how DAG/IP is built: end-users use the query protocols the access points support, and providers are contacted using the protocols the service access points support.

Three kinds of component make up the system. The Referral Index maintains the index of provider information and returns a list of reasonable referrals in answer to a search request; a referral is a pointer identifying providers that may hold information matching the query. The DAG-CAPs each provide one client access protocol: they receive a query in that protocol, convert it into a DAG/IP query for the Referral Index, and convert the answer back into the client's protocol, which may mean returning referrals directly, calling on the service access points to turn a referral into results, or both. The DAG-SAPs are called upon to pursue a referral by issuing the indicated query at the specified provider, and convert the results back into DAG/IP format; each handles referrals to providers speaking a particular protocol.

The memo draws two lessons from this arrangement. The first is that referrals and chaining are two distinct functions. The primary function of the system is to give users referrals to the providers that may hold what they are looking for; the chaining service, which pursues referrals the user's client software cannot handle itself, is a secondary support function. The second is that a single internal protocol and schema avoids an N by M mapping problem. With N possible client protocols and M possible provider protocols, mapping each pair directly would make the system complex and hard to extend, so the client access point knows only two protocols, its own and DAG/IP, and the service access point likewise. The access points and the service points are intended to be completely independent of each other, and each adjusts for differences in semantics between DAG/IP and its own protocol, which may mean post-filtering results or pruning them so that they match the original query more closely.
sections.plainLanguage: One internal language is used everywhere inside the system, and each piece translates between it and the protocol it faces. That way adding a new protocol means adding one module rather than one module for every combination. The main job is to point the user at the right provider; doing the search for them is the fallback.

sections.title: Running the Service
sections.content:
The service specifications start with availability. The primary designated client access points of all types, though not necessarily the secondary ones set up for load balancing, must be available to provide service or redirect queries on a 7x24 basis. Responses to queries should generally be available in under 10 seconds, though very generalised queries, where the user cannot specify enough to focus the search, can be deferred for much longer, because having results matters more than having them quickly. The data provided from each provider should be updated in the gateway at least once every 7 days.

Providers join by offering DAG-compatible access: access in exactly one of LDAPv2, LDAPv3 or Whois++, 7x24 service for answering referrals generated in the gateway, at least weekly updates of the index object describing the information their service indexes, the USER and ROLE templates for Whois++ servers and the inetorgperson and organizationalrole object classes for LDAP servers. Each compliant server is registered with details for each data set it covers: the host, port and protocol of the server, an identifier for the dataset, a URL for the service of preference for accessing the data, protocol-specific information, administrative contact information and the index object exchange information.

A provider that cannot meet these requirements may publish its data through an agreement with a third party that can, so data can be replicated between cooperating providers. The referral index does not claim ownership of personal information; it directs queries to the services that do own it, by whatever agreements with whichever parties. Load distribution is expected to be needed, since the system is anticipated to be popular: each part of the system must be replicable and service shared between replicas, and individual components may run on non-co-located hardware connected by TCP/IP networks. Large providers might be allowed to mirror the referral index or offer alternative access points and service points for their own personnel and customers; the memo says that is beyond its scope, but that the architecture was designed to support it.
sections.plainLanguage: The service has to answer quickly, stay up all the time and refresh its index at least weekly. A provider joins by offering its data in one of the three directory protocols and keeping it available. Every part of the gateway can be replicated, so the whole thing can be spread over several machines.

sections.title: Security and Data Integrity
sections.content:
In the context of read-only directory services, security is primarily about maintaining data integrity as it passes from the originating server to the end user. Some servers hold correct user information, and a client accessing a directory service should be certain that whichever servers the information passes through before reaching it, it receives a true representation of the original information. The DAG system as such must be completely invisible as the mediator of the information from the providers to the querying client. The only modifications that can appear are translations from one character set into another, which hopefully do not alter the meaning of the information.

In keeping with the public nature of the proposed service, the system does not provide any access control beyond each component's configuration to accept connections from recognised other components; for more detailed access control it is up to the connected providers to apply it. Since the system only supports searching and retrieving information, no updates can occur through the client access points. Security in the updates, that is the index objects, is provided by encryption and signature of objects from registered providers.
sections.plainLanguage: The gateway must not change the data it passes on, apart from translating character sets, so that the user gets exactly what the provider supplied. It offers no access control of its own beyond which components it accepts connections from, and providers are responsible for any finer control. Updates from providers are encrypted and signed.
